lessons.body:
## The three triggers

A component re-renders for exactly three reasons:

1. **Its own state changed.** `setState` / `useReducer` dispatch with a new value (`Object.is` comparison — setting the identical value bails out).
2. **Its parent re-rendered.** This is the big one: children re-render by default even when their props are byte-identical. Rendering cascades down the tree unless something stops it.
3. **A context it consumes changed value.** Only consumers of that context re-render — the rest of the tree is untouched.

## Re-render is not DOM update

Rendering means React called your component function again and built a new element tree. The commit phase then diffs and writes only what changed. A "wasted render" burns JavaScript time, not DOM time — but in a tree of thousands of components, JS time is the budget that blows first.

## The bailouts

- Setting state to the identical value (`Object.is`) skips the render entirely.
- `React.memo` skips a child whose props are shallow-unchanged.
- A stable `children` element (created above the re-rendering parent) lets React bail out on that subtree.

## The mental model to keep

Rendering is React calling your function again; reconciliation decides whether the DOM cares. Performance work is almost entirely about reducing how often functions get called, not about the DOM.
keyPoints: Three triggers: own state change, parent re-render, consumed context change.
Children re-render by default when the parent does, even with identical props.
Re-render (JS) is not commit (DOM) — wasted renders burn JS time.
Object.is bailout, memo, and stable children are the three escape hatches.
lessons.title: What Actually Triggers a Re-render

lessons.body:
## React.memo: skip renders with unchanged props

`memo(Component)` shallow-compares props and skips the render when nothing changed. It pays off for subtrees that re-render often with stable props — list rows, headers, sidebars. It does nothing when the parent passes fresh object literals or inline callbacks every render, because the shallow compare always fails.

## useMemo: cache expensive computations

```jsx
const total = useMemo(() => expensiveSum(items), [items]);
```

Use it for genuinely expensive derivations — not for cheap maps or object spreads. And treat it as a performance hint, not a semantic guarantee: React reserves the right to discard the cache.

## useCallback: referential stability

```jsx
const onSelect = useCallback((id) => setSelected(id), []);
```

Its job is keeping function identity stable across renders — for memoized children and for effect dependency arrays. Every `useCallback` is a small allocation plus a dependency list you must keep correct; stale closures are the tax.

## The cost of over-memoizing

Memoization is not free: the comparison itself costs, the cache costs memory, and the dependency lists cost correctness risk. The classic failure mode is a memoized parent whose inline props defeat the memo on every render — all cost, zero benefit, harder code to read.

## The rule

Profile first, memoize the hot path, and leave the rest alone. In newer React with the compiler, much of this is automated — know what it does so your manual memoization does not fight it.
keyPoints: memo skips renders on shallow-unchanged props; unstable props defeat it silently.
useMemo is for expensive derivations; useCallback is for stable references.
Every memo has a cost: comparison work, memory, and stale-closure risk.
Profile first; memoize hot paths, not everything.
lessons.title: memo, useMemo, useCallback — and Their Costs

lessons.body:
## The tool: React DevTools Profiler

Record an interaction, then read the flamegraph: wide bars are components that took long to render. "Highlight updates when components render" paints flashing borders on everything that re-rendered — the fastest way to see a cascade you did not expect.

## The workflow

1. Reproduce the slow interaction (typing in the search box, toggling a filter).
2. Record it in the Profiler.
3. Sort by render duration; find the widest bars.
4. For each, ask: *did this need to render?* If not, apply the fix: colocate the state lower, split the component, memoize with stable props, or virtualize the list.
5. Re-record and confirm the bars shrank.

## Render phase vs commit phase

The Profiler shows render-phase (JS) time per component. If the bars are thin but the interaction still janks, the cost is in the commit phase — DOM writes, layout, paint. That points at different fixes: fewer DOM nodes (virtualize), cheaper styles (avoid layout thrash), smaller trees.

## What "fixed" looks like

Typing in a search input re-renders the input and the results list — not the header, sidebar, and footer. That is the whole game: updates that stay local to the components that actually changed.
keyPoints: Profiler flamegraph + 'highlight updates' finds wasted renders fast.
Workflow: reproduce → record → widest bars → 'did this need to render?' → fix → re-record.
Thin bars but janky UI means commit-phase cost — look at DOM size and layout.
Fixed = updates stay local to components that actually changed.
lessons.title: Profiling: Finding Wasted Renders

lessons.body:
## Route-level splitting

```jsx
const Admin = lazy(() => import("./Admin"));
// ...
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <Admin />
</Suspense>
```

The dynamic `import()` becomes a separate bundle chunk, fetched on first render of `Admin`. Route-level splitting is the highest-leverage split in most apps: users download only the code for the page they are on.

## Component-level splitting

Heavy below-fold widgets — charts, rich editors, maps — can lazy-load on visibility (IntersectionObserver) or on intent (prefetch on hover). The trade-off is a network waterfall: a lazy component that fetches its own data after loading chains two round trips. Colocate the data fetch with the split, or prefetch early.

## Virtualization

For long lists, render only the visible window plus a small overscan buffer, and absolutely position rows inside a spacer of the full list height. The math is simple (see the exercise); the pitfalls are dynamic row heights, which need measurement, and scroll containers that must report their size honestly.

## Bundle vs runtime

Code splitting attacks bundle size (time to interactive); memoization and virtualization attack runtime cost (interaction jank). They solve different problems — profile to learn which one you have before reaching for either.
keyPoints: lazy + Suspense splits routes and heavy components into on-demand chunks.
Prefetch on intent to avoid the lazy-then-fetch waterfall.
Virtualization renders the visible window + overscan; dynamic heights need measurement.
Splitting fixes bundle size; memo/virtualization fix runtime — diagnose first.
lessons.title: Code Splitting and Virtualization

tagline: Re-renders are cheap until they aren't — learn what triggers them, how to prove they're wasted, and how to cut them.
